records.place: Château-Chalon, above the Seille valley, Jura

wine.name: Château-Chalon
wine.grapes: Savagnin alone, as the appellation requires.
wine.sites: The domaine's Savagnin on the steep grey and blue marl slopes below the village of Château-Chalon, perched on its cliff above the Seille, within the four communes the appellation covers.
wine.making: After fermentation the wine goes into old oak barrels that are never topped up or racked, so that a veil of yeast forms on its surface as it slowly evaporates. It stays there, in the family's old cellars in the heart of the village, for at least the sixty months under the veil the appellation asks, and is held until the December of the sixth year after the harvest before it is bottled in the clavelin.
wine.glass: Deep gold; walnut, curry spice, dried apple and toasted almond over brine and a smoky edge; bone dry and powerful at table wine strength, with high, cutting acidity and a very long, saline finish.
wine.ageing: Ready to drink on release, after more than six years, yet made to last: it gains depth for decades in a cool cellar.
wine.serve: 14 to 16 degrees Celsius, cool rather than cold; open it some hours ahead or decant it; a large white wine glass.

label.means: The appellation of 1936 for vin jaune alone, from Savagnin in four communes.
The squat 62 cl bottle of vin jaune, said to hold what is left of a litre after its years under the veil.

records.table: Domaine Jean Macle's Château-Chalon is vin jaune from the cliff village it is named for: Savagnin from marl slopes, aged untopped in old barrels under a veil of yeast for more than six years. Bone dry, nutty and saline, it wants opening hours ahead and a piece of Comté.
records.story: The Macle family has grown vines at Château-Chalon, the village on a cliff above the Seille, since 1850, as guides and merchants tell its history. Château-Chalon became an appellation in 1936, and it is the one appellation of the Jura reserved for vin jaune alone: Savagnin aged untopped under its veil of yeast for years. Its growers have shown how strictly they hold it. In years such as 1974, 1980, 1984 and 2001, when the harvest fell short of their standard, no wine was released under its name at all. In the 1960s the father of the present grower built the family's vines into the domaine that bears his name, and made its reputation. His son later took the domaine on and has kept its ways: Savagnin from the marl slopes below the village, old barrels, old cellars in the heart of the village, and long patience before release. The range is small, a few whites and a Macvin around the Château-Chalon. For a sommelier, Macle's Château-Chalon is the bottle to learn vin jaune by, and the one to set beside a fino Sherry: aged under a veil of yeast like it, yet never fortified.

others.name: Côtes du Jura Blanc
others.note: Chardonnay with some Savagnin, partly aged under the veil: the house style in a younger wine.

others.name: Macvin du Jura
others.note: The house's mistelle of unfermented grape must held with Jura marc, sweet and strong, poured cool as an aperitif.

traps: Château-Chalon is a village and an appellation for vin jaune alone, not a château: the domaine is Macle, and its wine is named for the place.
Vin jaune is never fortified: the veil of yeast forms on Savagnin at table wine strength, unlike fino Sherry.
Chardonnay or red wine grown inside the Château-Chalon boundary may not carry its name; it is sold as Côtes du Jura.

cards.front: Domaine Jean Macle's Château-Chalon: which grape, and how long under the veil at the least?
cards.back: Savagnin alone, at least sixty months untopped under the veil, held until the December of the sixth year after the harvest.

cards.front: Macle's appellation, Château-Chalon: what have its growers done when a harvest fell short?
cards.back: Released no wine under the name at all, as in 1974, 1980, 1984 and 2001.

questions.q: A guest is surprised that Domaine Jean Macle's Château-Chalon tastes of walnut and curry yet is not fortified. What gives it that character?
opts: Years untopped in barrel under a veil of yeast
A dose of grape spirit before it is aged
Grapes dried on straw mats for months
A solera of old and young wines
questions.exp: Savagnin left untopped for at least sixty months grows a film of yeast that gives walnut and curry notes; no spirit is added, so unlike fino Sherry it is never fortified.

questions.q: The harvest at Château-Chalon falls short of its growers' standard, as it did in 1984 and 2001. What has the appellation done in such years?
opts: Released no wine as Château-Chalon
Blended Chardonnay into the Savagnin
Released the wine after three years
Fortified the wine to help it keep
questions.exp: Its growers renounced the appellation in years such as 1974, 1980, 1984 and 2001; Chardonnay is never allowed in Château-Chalon, which is Savagnin alone.

report: Founded is left empty: guides and merchants give 1850 for the family at Château-Chalon, and 1964 or 1966 for the domaine as the father built it, so no one year is the founding.

The library's holdings line says the cellars are cut into the rock; the guides read describe old cellars beneath the village streets, and a forum note doubts the rock, so the record says beneath the village.

Left out for want of a second independent source: that the family came from a line of coopers, that the father led the growers' syndicate, that the house picks later than its neighbours, the age of its barrels (one account gives about forty years on average) and its time under the veil beyond the legal minimum (one account gives seven to seven and a half years).

The father is not named: no source read gave his dates, and one forum note reads as a tribute after his death without a date; he is the father of the present grower throughout. The son who took over in 1995 is living and is described, never named.
Living names for people.json, for the merge agent: the son who runs the domaine and his sister, both named in the importers' pages.
The organic certification year is left out: sources give 2015, 2019 and 2020.
Searches for this record: 6 of the group's 35, and one more shared with Château d'Arlay for the council's serving advice; the group used 30 in all.

changed: wine.making: "in the family's old cellars beneath the village,"; now "in the family's old cellars in the heart of the village,": No source read puts the cellars beneath the village; the Jura tourist board and a merchant describe cellars nestled in the heart of the village, one of them dating them to the sixteenth century.

story: "By the Jura wine council's account they declined to make it at all in years such as 1974, 1980, 1984 and 2001, when the harvest fell short of ..."; now "In years such as 1974, 1980, 1984 and 2001, when the harvest fell short of their standard, no wine was released under its name at all.": The four years stand (The Oxford Companion to Wine and a Swiss merchant's account of the appellation), but neither says the wine went unmade: the Oxford Companion says no wine was bottled under the name, the merchant that the vintage was declassified, so the wine was made and sold otherwise.

story: "In the 1960s the father of the present grower, who also served as mayor of the village, built up the family domaine, and he became known for his ..."; now "In the 1960s the father of the present grower built the family's vines into the domaine that bears his name, and made its reputation.": That he was mayor rests on the Guide Hachette alone among the sources read, and his grasp of the veil on none; the 1960s (1964 by Hachette, 1966 by another guide) and the reputation he made (the Wine Scholar Guild) stand on two.

story: "His son took the domaine on in 1995 and has kept its ways: Savagnin from the marl slopes below the village, old barrels, cool cellars beneath the ..."; now "His son later took the domaine on and has kept its ways: Savagnin from the marl slopes below the village, old barrels, old cellars in the heart of ...": The son's year is 1995 in two merchants' pages and 2003 in a French account, so no year is said; the cellars are placed as the sources place them.

cards.1.back: "Declined to make it at all, as in 1974, 1980, 1984 and 2001."; now "Released no wine under the name at all, as in 1974, 1980, 1984 and 2001.": In those years the wine was declassified and no wine bottled as Château-Chalon (The Oxford Companion to Wine, a Swiss merchant); it was not left unmade.
questions.1.opts.0: "Declined to make Château-Chalon at all"; now "Released no wine as Château-Chalon": The key now says what the sources say happened: no wine under the name, not no wine made.
open: That the father was mayor of Château-Chalon and led the growers' syndicate rests on the Guide Hachette alone among the sources read (a second page in the same results may be Hachette's own), so it is cut; a second independent source would restore it.
The year the son took the domaine on is 1995 in two merchants' pages and 2003 in a French account; it is not said.

The sixty months under the veil rest on the author's reading of the cahier through search and a sommelier school's summary of it (held until 15 December of the sixth year, at least sixty months under the veil); the INAO's own page read gives only more than six years under the veil. A modification of the cahier was opened to national opposition in February 2026, and whether it touches the ageing rule was not read.
The father has no dates in any source read, though one guide calls him the late Jean Macle; he stays described, never named in prose.

wine.name: Arbois-Pupillin Ploussard
wine.appellation: Arbois, with the village name Pupillin
wine.grapes: Poulsard alone, spelt Ploussard at Pupillin.
wine.sites: The house's own vines, all at Pupillin, the hilltop village a few kilometres south of Arbois that calls itself the capital of Ploussard.
wine.making: Made with no sulphur added at any stage, the house's custom since the mid 1980s, the Ploussard depends wholly on sound, ripe grapes and clean, careful work in the cellar, and it needs cool, steady keeping all the way from the cellar door to the glass.
wine.glass: Pale and translucent; cranberry, redcurrant and blood orange over rose petal and a dusty, savoury edge; almost weightless, with very light tannin, fresh acidity and a fine, clean finish.
wine.ageing: Open and lively young; kept cool and undisturbed all its life, as a wine with no added sulphur must be, it grows more savoury over ten years and more.
wine.serve: 12 to 14 degrees Celsius; no need to decant, though a little air helps a closed bottle; a Burgundy glass.

label.means: The Arbois appellation with the village name Pupillin added, not an appellation of its own.
Pupillin's spelling of Poulsard, the Jura's pale, thin skinned red grape.

records.table: Domaine Pierre Overnoy's Ploussard is a pale red from Pupillin, the Arbois village that spells Poulsard its own way, made with no added sulphur since the mid 1980s. Light, translucent and fresh, with cranberry and blood orange, it wants a cool cellar and a cool pour.
records.story: The house works a small family estate at Pupillin, the hilltop village above Arbois that calls itself the capital of Ploussard. The grower whose name the house bears took over his family's vines there in 1968. As the story is usually told, he found his way in the cellar through the ideas of Jules Chauvet (1907 to 1989), the Beaujolais négociant and chemist who studied the yeasts of the grape and warned against the heavy use of sulphur. By the mid 1980s he had stopped adding sulphur to his wines, and the house has made them without it ever since. His pale, almost weightless Ploussard became a red that the natural wine movement looks to. He passed the domaine to the young man who had worked beside him since about 1990, often called his adopted son, and that successor and his wife have carried it on, with the same vines and the same ways. For a sommelier, Overnoy's Ploussard teaches two things at once: the Jura's own pale red grape, and what a wine made with nothing added can be when the grapes and the cellar are clean.

others.name: Arbois Pupillin Chardonnay
others.note: Chardonnay topped up in cask, so fresh rather than oxidative.

others.name: Arbois Pupillin Savagnin
others.note: Savagnin made in either idiom, topped up or under the veil, depending on the cuvée.

traps: Ploussard and Poulsard are one grape: Pupillin spells it Ploussard, and the rest of the Jura Poulsard.
Arbois Pupillin is the Arbois appellation with the village name added, not a separate appellation.
Its pale colour is the nature of the grape, thin skinned and large berried, not a sign of a rosé or of a weak year.

cards.front: Domaine Pierre Overnoy: what does the house leave out of its wines, and since when?
cards.back: Added sulphur, at every stage, since the mid 1980s.

cards.front: Which grape is Overnoy's Ploussard, and why is it spelt that way on the label?
cards.back: Poulsard, the Jura's pale red grape; Ploussard is the spelling of Pupillin, the village of the vines.

questions.q: A guest orders Domaine Pierre Overnoy's Ploussard and asks which grape it is. Which answer fits?
opts: Poulsard, under Pupillin's own spelling
Trousseau, the Jura's darker red
Pinot Noir grown on Jura marl
Savagnin pressed as a light red
questions.exp: Ploussard is Pupillin's spelling of Poulsard, the pale, thin skinned red; Trousseau is the Jura's other native red, darker and firmer.

questions.q: As the story is usually told, whose ideas, those of a Beaujolais négociant and chemist, led the grower behind Domaine Pierre Overnoy to give up added sulphur?
opts: Jules Chauvet
Louis Pasteur
Émile Peynaud
Jules Guyot
questions.exp: Jules Chauvet (1907 to 1989) studied the yeasts of the grape and warned against the heavy use of sulphur; Louis Pasteur, who grew up in Arbois, studied fermentation a century earlier.

sources.title: Louis/Dressner Selections: Overnoy producer page
Grandi Bottiglie: Overnoy producer page
Wine Scholar Guild: Jura producer guide
Wikipedia: Jules Chauvet
More Than Organic: Jules Chauvet

report: The making rests on what two sources agree: no added sulphur since the early 1980s (one guide gives 1983; another 1984 for the fermentation and 1986 for bottling, so the two steps are left out). One merchant's sheet for the 2018 vintage gives natural yeasts and an élevage on fine lees in stainless steel, while a wiki speaks of old oak; neither is confirmed, so the vessel, the yeasts and the length of élevage are left out.
The Wine Scholar Guild is cited by its Jura index, because the address of its Overnoy entry, like Raisin's, names the living successor; the facts are read from that entry.

Left out for want of a second source: the meeting with a disciple of Chauvet, Chauvet as mentor and friend (one source each), the year the successor returned to work full time (1997 in the importer's profile), the planting of Trousseau in 2013, and the six hectares.
The library's style line says no added sulphur at any stage with long élevage; the first half is borne out, the long élevage is not confirmed for the Ploussard and is not said.

The grower whose name the house bears and his successor are living and are described, never named. Living names for people.json, for the merge agent: the adopted son and successor, his wife, and the Chauvet disciple named in one guide.
Searches for this record: 6 of the group's 35, and one fetch of the importer's profile, refused.

changed: wine.making: "the house's custom since the early 1980s,"; now "the house's custom since the mid 1980s,": By the grower's own account in an importer's interview, part of the 1985 vintage and all of 1986 were made without sulphur; guides give 1983 and 1984. The mid 1980s holds for all of them; the early 1980s for one.

table: "made with no added sulphur since the early 1980s."; now "made with no added sulphur since the mid 1980s.": As for the making: 1985 in part and 1986 in full by the grower's own account, 1984 in one guide.

story: "He found his way in the cellar through the ideas of Jules Chauvet"; now "As the story is usually told, he found his way in the cellar through the ideas of Jules Chauvet": The Chauvet line is the usual telling (an importer's and a merchant's accounts, one of them through a follower of Chauvet in the early 1980s), but the grower's own account starts closer to home, so it is told as the usual telling.

story: "In the early 1980s he stopped adding sulphur to his wines, and the house has made them without it ever since."; now "By the mid 1980s he had stopped adding sulphur to his wines, and the house has made them without it ever since.": 1985 in part and 1986 in full by the grower's own account, 1984 in one guide: the mid 1980s.

story: "He later adopted a young man who came to work beside him, and that adopted son and his wife have carried the domaine on, with the same vines and ..."; now "He passed the domaine to the young man who had worked beside him since about 1990, often called his adopted son, and that successor and his wife ...": Several accounts call the successor his adopted son, another his spiritual son, and none read records an adoption; he joined for the 1989 harvest by one account and in 1990 by another, so about 1990. The handover year (1999 or 2001) is not said.
cards.0.back: "Added sulphur, at every stage, since the early 1980s."; now "Added sulphur, at every stage, since the mid 1980s.": As for the making and the story.

questions.1.q: "Whose teaching, a Beaujolais négociant and chemist's, led the grower behind Domaine Pierre Overnoy to make wine without added sulphur?"; now "As the story is usually told, whose ideas, those of a Beaujolais négociant and chemist, led the grower behind Domaine Pierre Overnoy to give up ...": The stem now hedges the Chauvet line as the usual telling, as the story does, so the one key stays right against the grower's own account.

questions.0.exp: "Trousseau is the Jura's darker, firmer red, grown mostly on warmer gravels."; now "Trousseau is the Jura's other native red, darker and firmer.": That Trousseau grows mostly on warmer gravels was read in no source, and Wikipedia gives the limestone of Montigny-lès-Arsures, the village that calls itself the capital of Trousseau, as the soil said to suit it; the clause is cut and the grape kept.
open: By the grower's own account in an importer's interview, his father made wine without sulphur before him; that rests on the one account, so the story tells the Chauvet line only as the usual telling and says nothing of the father.
The guides read call the house Maison Pierre Overnoy; the plan's name Domaine Pierre Overnoy is kept, for the read-together agent.
The handover year (1999 or 2001) and whether the adoption was a legal one were not settled; neither is said.
The record still cites no primary source; the Jura wine council's Pupillin sheet, read through search, bears out the capital of Ploussard and is listed in the review.

wine.name: Arbois Chardonnay Les Bruyères
wine.grapes: Chardonnay alone, from a single parcel.
wine.sites: Les Bruyères, a parcel facing due south on heavy Triassic clay over a subsoil of blue marl, with old vines, some planted as early as 1938, farmed biodynamically.
wine.making: Fermented with its own yeasts in 228 litre oak barrels, about a fifth of them new, it then rests on its lees in the same barrels for about two years, kept topped up so that no veil of yeast forms, before it is bottled.
wine.glass: Lemon peel, ripe pear and a hint of hazelnut over a cool, stony edge and a light touch of toasted oak; taut, dry and pure, with high acidity, a fine texture from the lees and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Taut and closed in its first years, it gains breadth and depth with age and keeps for many years in a cool cellar.
wine.serve: 10 to 13 degrees Celsius; a young bottle gains from an hour in a decanter; a Burgundy white wine glass.

label.means: The northern commune appellation of the Jura, granted in 1936, for every colour and style.
The single parcel, on clay over blue marl, whose grapes the domaine bottles apart.

records.table: Domaine André et Mireille Tissot's Les Bruyères is an Arbois Chardonnay from one south facing parcel on clay over blue marl, aged two years in barrel on its lees and kept topped up. It tastes fresh and taut rather than nutty, the Jura's other white idiom.
records.story: Domaine André et Mireille Tissot was founded in 1962 at Montigny-lès-Arsures, the village beside Arbois that calls itself the capital of Trousseau, by the couple whose names it bears. In time their son, trained at Beaune, took the domaine on, and it changed its farming and its range. The family turned to organic farming, certified by 1999, then to biodynamic farming, certified from 2004 across all its appellations, and began to bottle its Chardonnay parcel by parcel. Les Bruyères, a south facing slope of heavy Triassic clay over blue marl planted with old vines, became one of those single parcel Chardonnays, aged in barrel on its lees for about two years and kept topped up, so that no veil forms. The domaine kept its vin jaune and its other veiled wines beside them, along with Crémant du Jura and vin de paille, so that one cellar makes both Juras: the topped up, fresh idiom and the oxidative one under the veil. For a sommelier, Les Bruyères is the wine to pour beside a vin jaune of the same house, to show a guest what Jura Chardonnay becomes when it is topped up and grown on a named parcel.

others.name: Arbois Vin Jaune
others.note: Savagnin aged untopped under the veil and sold in the clavelin: the house's oxidative face.

others.name: Arbois La Tour de Curon
others.note: Another of the house's single parcel Chardonnays, bottled apart.

others.name: Crémant du Jura
others.note: Traditional method sparkling wine, mostly Chardonnay, made with the same care as the house's other wines.

traps: Les Bruyères is topped up, ouillé, so it has none of the nutty, veil aged character of the house's vin jaune.
Montigny-lès-Arsures is the domaine's village, inside the Arbois appellation; it is not an appellation of its own.
Les Bruyères is a parcel name, not a grape or a style: the wine is Chardonnay alone.

cards.front: Tissot's Les Bruyères: what soil lies under the parcel, and which way does it face?
cards.back: Heavy Triassic clay over a subsoil of blue marl, facing due south.

cards.front: Domaine André et Mireille Tissot: when was it founded, and from when is its biodynamic farming certified?
cards.back: Founded in 1962 at Montigny-lès-Arsures; certified biodynamic from 2004.

questions.q: A guest who loves vin jaune is poured Tissot's Les Bruyères and finds no nutty note at all. Why?
opts: It is topped up in barrel, so no veil forms
It is made from Savagnin rather than Chardonnay
It is raised in steel tanks for a few months
It is a sparkling wine of the traditional method
questions.exp: Les Bruyères is a Chardonnay kept topped up in barrel, so no veil of yeast forms and it stays fresh; it spends about two years in barrel, not a few months in steel.

questions.q: In what year did the couple whose names Domaine André et Mireille Tissot bears found the estate at Montigny-lès-Arsures?
questions.exp: The domaine was founded in 1962; 1936 is the year of the Arbois appellation, and 2004 the year its biodynamic farming was first certified.

report: The domaine's own technical sheet for Les Bruyères (an early vintage) gives the same soil, aspect, barrels, new oak share and two years on lees as the merchants cited, with very low sulphur and twenty years of keeping; it is not cited because the domaine's own address carries the first name of the living son, so the record stands on the merchants and guides that agree with it, and the low sulphur and twenty years are left out.
The library's holdings line puts the single parcel Chardonnays on marl and limestone; for Les Bruyères the sheet and the merchants give Triassic clay over blue marl, which the record follows.

Founded 1962 rests on two merchants' histories; the library gives no year. The son's start is given as 1980, 1989 and 1990 by different sources, so no year is said; his training at Beaune rests on two accounts (Beaune, Burgundy).
Organic certification by 1999 and Demeter certification in 2004 rest on two sources each; native yeasts for Les Bruyères rest on one merchant and are left out.

The founders, whose names the house bears, are described as the couple; no source read gave their dates or said whether they are living. The son and his wife are living and never named; both names are for people.json, for the merge agent.
Searches for this record: 6 of the group's 35.

changed: wine.making: "Fermented in 228 litre oak barrels,"; now "Fermented with its own yeasts in 228 litre oak barrels,": The spontaneous fermentation with the grapes' own yeasts is now in two merchants' sheets (Comptoir des Millésimes, and the author's Vino al Vino), so it is added.

story: "the village just north of Arbois that claims Trousseau as its own grape,"; now "the village beside Arbois that calls itself the capital of Trousseau,": Wikipedia and the Jura tourist board's Trousseau trail give the title capital of Trousseau and a village adjoining Arbois; no source read gave its bearing from the town.
open: The son's start is 1990 in three accounts read here, against 1980 and 1989 in the author's; it is still not said. 1990 is a distractor in the story question, which asks the founding year, so it is not a second right answer.
Montigny-lès-Arsures lies north of Arbois on the map, but no source read gave the bearing, so the record says beside Arbois.
The record cites no primary source: the domaine's own sheet, whose address names the living son, agrees with the merchants for the soil, the barrels and the lees.

wine.name: Vin de Paille
wine.grapes: Chardonnay and Savagnin with the red Poulsard and Trousseau.
wine.sites: The estate's vineyards on the slopes around the village of Arlay, below the ruins of its medieval fortress, some ten kilometres from Château-Chalon in the Côtes du Jura.
wine.making: Bunches picked ripe and free of rot are laid on racks to dry for three to four months, well beyond the six weeks the appellation asks; more than three kilograms of grapes go into each half bottle. The pressed juice ferments and the wine is then aged for three or four years in small oak casks before bottling, by the estate's pages.
wine.glass: Deep amber gold; dried apricot, quince paste, candied orange peel and honey over toasted almond and caramel; rich and sweet, yet lifted by fresh acidity, with a long, clean finish.
wine.ageing: Ready when it is released after its years in cask, it keeps for decades, its fruit turning towards caramel, dried fig and gingerbread.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius, well chilled; no need to decant; a small white wine glass, poured a little at a time.

label.means: Straw wine: sweet wine from grapes dried for at least six weeks after picking, never fortified.
The regional appellation of 1937, for every colour and style along the whole Jura vineyard.

records.table: Château d'Arlay's Vin de Paille is the sweet wine of the Côtes du Jura: Chardonnay, Savagnin, Poulsard and Trousseau dried on racks for months, then aged three or four years in oak. Amber, honeyed and fresh, it wants a cold pour and a small glass.
records.story: Château d'Arlay stands below the ruins of a medieval fortress some ten kilometres from Château-Chalon, and by its own account its vineyard appears in archives of the eleventh century, which leads it to call itself the oldest château vineyard in France. Tradition gives the first fortifications to the ninth century. In the 1260s the lordship passed to the first of the Chalon-Arlay line, a branch of the house of Chalon whose fortune rested on the salt works of Salins-les-Bains; the fortress grew under them, and the estate later came down through the princes of Orange. Around 1770 a countess who held the barony bought the old convent of the Minimes at the foot of the ruins and, over nearly ten years, made it the château and the romantic park that visitors see. She was guillotined in 1794, and her grandson, of the Arenberg family, took the estate back in 1825. From 1960 the Laguiche family, father and then son, developed the wine estate and opened the château to visitors. The house has long been known for vin jaune and for vin de paille, the sweet wine of grapes dried for months before pressing. For a sommelier, Arlay's Vin de Paille is the Jura's sweet idiom, rich without any fortification.

others.name: Vin Jaune
others.note: Côtes du Jura Savagnin aged untopped under the veil for more than six years and sold in the clavelin.

others.name: Corail
others.note: A Côtes du Jura red from the Jura's three red and two white grapes, fermented and macerated together.

traps: Vin de paille owes its sweetness to dried grapes, not to added spirit: the Jura's fortified wine is Macvin du Jura, must held with marc.
Vin de paille is a mention under the geographic appellations, here Côtes du Jura, not an appellation of its own.
Arlay lies in the Côtes du Jura, some ten kilometres from Château-Chalon; it is not one of the four communes of that appellation, which allows vin jaune alone.

cards.front: Château d'Arlay's Vin de Paille: how long are its grapes dried, and on what?
cards.back: Three to four months on racks, by the estate's account, well beyond the six weeks the appellation asks.

cards.front: Which line took the lordship of Château d'Arlay in the 1260s, and where did its fortune come from?
cards.back: The Chalon-Arlay line, a branch of the house of Chalon grown rich on the salt works of Salins-les-Bains.

questions.q: A guest asks how Château d'Arlay's Vin de Paille becomes sweet without any added spirit. Which answer fits?
opts: Its grapes are dried on racks for months
Its grapes are frozen on the vine
Its grapes are touched by noble rot
Its must is held with Jura marc
questions.exp: The bunches dry on racks for three to four months, concentrating sugar and acid; adding marc to must makes Macvin du Jura, not vin de paille.

questions.q: Château d'Arlay traces its vineyard to the Middle Ages. In the 1260s its lordship passed to which line, enriched by salt?
opts: The Chalon-Arlay line
The Dukes of Burgundy
The Habsburg emperors
The Counts of Champagne
questions.exp: In the 1260s the estate passed to the Chalon-Arlay line, a branch of a house grown rich on the salt of Salins; the princes of Orange came later, by descent.

report: The house's history rests on its own history page (the ninth century fortifications as tradition, 1269, the princes of Orange, the countess's château of about 1770, 1794, 1825 and the family's wine estate from 1960), hedged as its account; the claim to be the oldest château vineyard in France is the estate's own. A science glossary page also calls it the oldest château vineyard in France, so the claim stands as the estate's, hedged.
The countess (the comtesse de Lauraguais), the founder of the Chalon-Arlay line and her Arenberg grandson are described, not named, because no source read gave their dates in two places.

The Laguiche family is named as a family only: the father who began in 1960, his son and the grandson who now runs the estate are not named; the son and grandson are living and their names are for people.json, for the merge agent. The year of the latest handover differs between sources (2022 and 2024) and is left out.
Founded is empty: the estate is older than any founding date.
Vineyard sizes differ between sources (16, 22, 25 and 30 hectares) and are left out as volatile.
Searches for this record: 7 of the group's 35, and one shared with Domaine Jean Macle.

changed: wine.sites: "south of Château-Chalon in the Côtes du Jura."; now "some ten kilometres from Château-Chalon in the Côtes du Jura.": Arlay is not south of Château-Chalon: the two lie at about the same latitude, Arlay to the west, and the Jura tourist board puts Arlay some ten kilometres from Château-Chalon.

wine.making: "Bunches picked fully ripe are sorted by hand, one by one, then laid on racks"; now "Bunches picked ripe and free of rot are laid on racks": The estate's pages read say the grapes are picked ripe and always free of rot; the sorting one by one was not read in them or elsewhere.

wine.making: "The pressed juice ferments and the wine is then aged for some four years in oak casks before bottling."; now "The pressed juice ferments and the wine is then aged for three or four years in small oak casks before bottling, by the estate's pages.": The estate's product page gives four years in oak casks and its older page on the wines three years in small casks; both are now given as the estate's.
table: "then aged some four years in oak."; now "then aged three or four years in oak.": As for the making: the estate's pages give three and four years.

story: "a medieval fortress south of Château-Chalon,"; now "a medieval fortress some ten kilometres from Château-Chalon,": As for the sites: Arlay lies west of Château-Chalon, not south, some ten kilometres from it.

story: "In 1269 the lordship passed to the Chalon-Arlay line, whose wealth from the salt works of Salins-les-Bains built the fortress and widened the ..."; now "In the 1260s the lordship passed to the first of the Chalon-Arlay line, a branch of the house of Chalon whose fortune rested on the salt works of ...": The estate's history page gives 1269, its own visit page and Wikipedia's account of the first lord of the line 1266, so the 1260s. The salt fortune of the house of Chalon stands on Wikipedia's history of Jura salt and a heritage synthesis; that it widened the vineyard was read in no second source.
traps.2: "Arlay lies in the Côtes du Jura, south of Château-Chalon;"; now "Arlay lies in the Côtes du Jura, some ten kilometres from Château-Chalon;": As for the sites: not south of Château-Chalon.

cards.1.front: "Which line took the lordship of Château d'Arlay in 1269, and where did its wealth come from?"; now "Which line took the lordship of Château d'Arlay in the 1260s, and where did its fortune come from?": 1269 and 1266 are both the estate's; the card asks for the decade. Wave two holds no frozen id, so the new front orphans nothing.

cards.1.back: "The Chalon-Arlay line, enriched by the salt works of Salins-les-Bains."; now "The Chalon-Arlay line, a branch of the house of Chalon grown rich on the salt works of Salins-les-Bains.": The salt fortune was the house of Chalon's, from Salins, which the line shared as its branch.

questions.1.q: "In 1269 its lordship passed to which line, enriched by salt?"; now "In the 1260s its lordship passed to which line, enriched by salt?": 1269 and 1266 are both given by the estate; the stem asks for the decade.

questions.1.exp: "In 1269 the estate passed to the Chalon-Arlay line, whose salt wealth from Salins built its fortress; the princes of Orange came later, by descent."; now "In the 1260s the estate passed to the Chalon-Arlay line, a branch of a house grown rich on the salt of Salins; the princes of Orange came later, ...": As for the story and the stem.
open: The ninth century tradition and the eleventh century archives are the estate's alone and are hedged as its account; the claim to be the oldest château vineyard in France is the estate's (premier château vignoble de France, and the oldest wine château in France, on its pages), told as what it calls itself.
That the Chalon-Arlay line widened the vineyard, the author's reading of the estate's history page, is cut for want of a second source.

The countess, comtesse de Lauraguais and baroness of Arlay from 1767 to 1789 by the estate, guillotined in 1794, could be named with her dates if a second source gives her birth year; she stays described.

The six weeks of drying the appellation asks rest on the author's reading of the cahier and the Jura tourist board's account of vin de paille; the INAO's opposition text for Arbois lists the four grapes allowed.

wine.name: Arbois Savagnin Ouillé
wine.sites: A blend of the domaine's Savagnin parcels in the Arbois appellation; its Grand Curoulet parcel, on grey and mottled marls, is bottled apart.
wine.making: The grapes are lightly crushed and pressed, and the juice ferments in barrels and foudres. The wine is then aged for ten months to a year in 500 litre barrels and foudres, kept topped up so that no veil of yeast forms, with new oak held to a small share.
wine.glass: Lemon zest, green apple and quince over a hint of fresh almond and a salty, stony edge; taut and dry, with high, bright acidity, a fine texture and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Open and bright when young, it holds and gains breadth for several years in a cool cellar.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white Burgundy glass.

label.means: The northern commune appellation of the Jura, granted in 1936, for every colour and style.
Savagnin topped up in cask, so fresh and fruit led, with no veil character.

records.table: Domaine du Pélican's Arbois Savagnin Ouillé shows the Jura's own white grape without the veil: fermented and aged about a year in large barrels and foudres, kept topped up so it stays fresh. Taut, lemony and long, it lets a guest meet Savagnin before vin jaune.
records.story: Domaine du Pélican is the Jura estate of the family behind Domaine Marquis d'Angerville in Volnay, in Burgundy. By the domaine's account, the family began looking for land in the Jura in 2007, guided by a soil geologist, and in 2012 it founded the estate with its first purchases: the Château de Chavannes and its vines at Montigny-lès-Arsures, and the Grand Curoulet vineyard at Arbois. It took its name from the pelican, the emblem of the town of Arbois. In 2015 a retiring grower of the Arbois appellation entrusted his vines to the estate, which bought them in 2018, by the domaine's account. The family farms biodynamically, and in 2020 built a new cellar into the slope beside the Château de Chavannes at Montigny-lès-Arsures. It has bottled Savagnin topped up since its first vintage, and its range sets it beside a Savagnin under the veil and a vin jaune, the two idioms of the Jura side by side. For a sommelier, the Savagnin Ouillé is the clean way to teach the grape itself, before a guest meets it under the veil.

others.name: Arbois Grand Curoulet Savagnin Ouillé
others.note: Topped up Savagnin from the single Grand Curoulet parcel on grey and mottled marls, a third of it left overnight on its skins.

traps: Domaine du Pélican is a separate estate in the Jura, not a wine of Domaine Marquis d'Angerville in Volnay, though one family stands behind both.
Ouillé means topped up: this Savagnin never ages under the veil, unlike the domaine's vin jaune from the same grape.
The pelican of its name is the emblem of the town of Arbois, not a vineyard or a place name.

cards.front: Domaine du Pélican's Savagnin Ouillé: what does ouillé mean, and what does it change?
cards.back: Topped up in cask, so no veil of yeast forms and the Savagnin stays fresh rather than nutty.

cards.front: Which Volnay domaine's family founded Domaine du Pélican, and in what year?
cards.back: The family of Domaine Marquis d'Angerville, in 2012.

questions.q: A guest tastes Domaine du Pélican's Arbois Savagnin Ouillé beside its vin jaune and asks why the two differ so. What is the reason?
opts: The ouillé is topped up, so no veil forms
The ouillé is made from Chardonnay instead
The vin jaune is fortified with grape spirit
The vin jaune is made from dried grapes
questions.exp: Both are Savagnin; the ouillé is topped up in barrel and stays fresh, while the vin jaune ages untopped under a veil of yeast and is never fortified.

questions.q: In what year was Domaine du Pélican founded at Montigny-lès-Arsures by a family of Volnay?
questions.exp: It was founded in 2012; the family began looking for land in 2007, took on a retiring grower's old vines in 2015 and opened its new cellar in 2020.

report: The retiring grower whose vines the domaine took on is living and is described, not named; the domaine's own history gives 2015 for the vines entrusted and 2018 for the purchase, one merchant 2015 and another 2014, so the record follows the domaine.

The soil geologist who guided the search from 2007 is named on the domaine's page and may be living, so he is described; the two founders, the Volnay family's head (in people.json) and his long serving manager, are never named, and the manager's name is for people.json, for the merge agent.
The élevage of the Savagnin Ouillé is about twelve months by the domaine's page and ten months by two merchants' sheets for other vintages, hence ten months to a year.
The legend behind the pelican of Arbois's arms (a pet of Mary of Burgundy) is in one source only and is left out.
The domaine's page names Grand Curoulet at Arbois and the Château de Chavannes at Montigny as its first purchases; the library's Grand Curoulet Chardonnay agrees.
Searches for this record: 4 of the group's 35.

changed: story: "It took its name from the pelican on the arms of the town of Arbois."; now "It took its name from the pelican, the emblem of the town of Arbois.": The domaine's history page calls the pelican the emblem of the town of Arbois; no source read described the town's arms.

story: "entrusted his old vines to the estate,"; now "entrusted his vines to the estate,": The domaine's page gives the vines entrusted in 2015 and bought in 2018, about five hectares; their age was read in no source.

story: "and in 2020 opened a new cellar in the Clos Saint Laurent at Montigny-lès-Arsures."; now "and in 2020 built a new cellar into the slope beside the Château de Chavannes at Montigny-lès-Arsures.": The domaine's page dates the new cellar to 2020; two importers place it on the first purchase at Montigny, built into the slope by the Château de Chavannes, with the Clos Saint Laurent behind it, not in it.
traps.2: "the emblem on the arms of the town of Arbois,"; now "the emblem of the town of Arbois,": As for the story: the domaine says emblem, and no source read described the arms.
open: The domaine's page says the search outside Burgundy began in 2006 and turned to the Jura after a blind tasting in 2007; the record's 2007 stands for the Jura.
Whether the soil geologist who guided the search is living was not settled; he stays described.
